summary: Assign non-negative heights so water is 0 and adjacent cells differ by at most 1, maximising the highest peak.
mainInsight: A cell can be no higher than its distance to the nearest water, and setting every cell to exactly that distance satisfies all rules. So run a multi-source BFS from all water cells.
invariant: When a cell is first reached, its height is its step distance to the nearest water cell, which is the maximum height it can take.
canonicalApproach: Multi-source BFS from all water cells

approaches.summary: Search for the nearest water per cell.

approaches.summary: Enqueue all water at height 0 and expand.

personalSolution.approach: Multi-source BFS from all water cells, writing heights into the input grid
personalSolution.notes: Optimal. The seen set of tuples is heavier than a -1-filled height matrix, and the level loop is not needed since heights come from the parent.

commonMistakes: Not seeing that this is 01 Matrix in disguise.
BFS from a single water cell instead of all of them.
Using DFS, which can assign heights that break the difference rule.
edgeCases: Single water cell in a corner of a large map.

promptVariants: Why is each cell's distance to the nearest water both an upper bound and achievable?
Prove that BFS distances give the maximum peak.
cards.answer: Upper bound: along a shortest path of d steps from the nearest water, height can rise by at most 1 per step, so height <= d. Achievable: assigning every cell its distance d works, because adjacent cells' distances differ by at most 1 and water gets 0. Every cell is simultaneously at its maximum, so the peak is maximised.
keyPoints: Height rises at most 1 per step from water
Distances of neighbours differ by at most 1
All cells at their own maximum at once
cards.explanation: Showing a bound and an assignment that meets it is the standard optimality argument.

promptVariants: One row with water only at the left end: [[1, 0, 0, 0]]. Heights?
cards.explanation: Heights equal the distance to the only water cell, increasing by 1 per step.

incorrectOptionExplanations.[[0, 1, 1, 1]]: Valid but not maximal; the peak can be 3.
incorrectOptionExplanations.[[0, 1, 2, 1]]: Nothing forces the last cell down; there is no water on the right.

promptVariants: Why does a BFS from just one water cell fail?
What goes wrong if only the first water cell found is used as the BFS source?
options: Cells near other water get heights that are too high
Water cells further away would be set below 0
The BFS would never reach all land cells
It only fails when water cells are adjacent
cards.answer: Cells near other water get heights that are too high
cards.explanation: A land cell next to a different water cell must be at most 1, but single-source BFS assigns its distance to the chosen source.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Water cells further away would be set be: BFS only increases heights; the error is that heights get too large.
incorrectOptionExplanations.The BFS would never reach all land cells: It reaches all cells; the values are wrong.
incorrectOptionExplanations.It only fails when water cells are adjac: It fails whenever there are two separate water sources.

promptVariants: What is the time complexity of the canonical code?

options: O(m * n * W), W water cells
cards.explanation: Each cell is assigned and enqueued once and checks 4 neighbours.

incorrectOptionExplanations.O((m * n)^2): That is a BFS per cell.
incorrectOptionExplanations.O(m * n * W), W water cells: All water cells share one BFS.
incorrectOptionExplanations.O(m * n * log(m * n)): No priority queue; unit steps need only a deque.
